solution: Quartile deviation = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2, so Q3 = Q1 + 2 × 8 = 104 + 16 = 120.

subject: DA
q: What's the probability of drawing a red card or a card with a face from a standard deck of 52 cards?
solution: 26 red cards plus 12 face cards, minus the 6 red face cards counted twice: 32 cards. 32/52 = 8/13.

q: The median of the dataset {4, 8, 15, 14, 23, 42} is ____
solution: In order: 4, 8, 14, 15, 23, 42. The middle two are 14 and 15, so the median is 14.5.

solution: A discrete random variable takes separate, countable values, usually whole numbers such as 0, 1, 2, rather than any value in a range.

solution: A line graph plots numerical values so differences and changes are easy to compare, especially over time.

subject: DA
q: A deck of cards has 52 cards, of which 13 are clubs. What is the probability of drawing a club?
solution: 13 clubs out of 52 cards: 13/52 = 1/4 = 0.25.

subject: DA
q: To illustrate the percentage distribution of various departments in a company, which graph would be most effective?
solution: A pie chart shows how a whole splits into parts, such as departments as percentages of a company.

subject: DA
q: Independent events: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.2. What is the probability of A given B?
solution: For independent events, knowing B happened changes nothing: P(A | B) = P(A) = 0.3.

subject: DA
q: The median of a dataset is 25. If the dataset is: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, what is the value of the 3rd quartile?
showNote: The median of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is 30, not 25. Taking the upper half as 30, 40, 50 gives 40; methods that leave out the median give 45.
solution: The third quartile is the middle of the upper half. With the upper half 30, 40, 50, that is 40.

subject: DA
q: Calculate the median of the data set: 6, 3, 8, 2, 9, 1

subject: DA
q: In a region with a 0.4 chance of rain per day, what is the probability of 3 consecutive dry days?
solution: P(dry) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6 each day, so three dry days in a row: 0.6³ = 0.216 = 21.6%.

subject: DA
q: Surveys are what data collection method?
solution: A survey collects new data directly from people, so it is a primary method.

solution: 4 fives and 4 sevens: 8/52 = 2/13.

q: In a class of 40 students, 25 like math and 20 like science. How many students like both math and science?
solution: 25 + 20 = 45, which is 5 more than the 40 students, so 5 like both (if every student likes at least one).

subject: DA
q: If covariance is 40 and correlation is 0.8, with X's standard deviation 5, what is the standard deviation?
solution: Correlation r = covariance ÷ (σX × σY), so σX × σY = 40 ÷ 0.8 = 50. The question means the standard deviation of Y, because X's is already given as 5. So σY = 50 ÷ 5 = 10.
trick: 40 ÷ 0.8 is 400 ÷ 8 = 50, which is the product of the two standard deviations. Then 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

subject: DA
q: The range of a dataset is 24, and the highest value is 42. What is the lowest?
solution: Range = highest − lowest, so lowest = highest − range = 42 − 24 = 18.
trick: Subtract in two steps: 42 − 20 = 22, then 22 − 4 = 18.

subject: DA
q: A binomial distribution has n = 400 trials and p = 0.5 success probability. Calculate the standard deviation.
solution: For a binomial distribution, standard deviation = √(npq). Here n = 400, p = 0.5 and q = 0.5, so √(400 × 0.5 × 0.5) = √100 = 10.
trick: When p = 0.5, npq = n ÷ 4, so the standard deviation is √n ÷ 2. √400 = 20, and half of 20 is 10. The option 20 forgets to halve.

subject: DA
q: The interquartile range of exam scores is 10. If the first quartile is 20, what is the third quartile?
solution: Interquartile range = Q3 − Q1, so Q3 = Q1 + IQR = 20 + 10 = 30.
trick: Q3 is just Q1 plus the IQR: 20 + 10 = 30.

subject: DA
q: A pie chart's largest sector is 144 degrees. What percentage of the total does it represent?
solution: A full circle is 360°, so the share is 144 ÷ 360 × 100% = 40%.
trick: Every 36° is 10% of the circle, and 144 ÷ 36 = 4, so the sector is 40%.

subject: DA
q: A dataset has a standard deviation of 5. If each value is increased by 10, what is the new standard deviation?
solution: Standard deviation measures how far values sit from the mean. Adding 10 to every value moves the mean up by 10 as well, so every distance from the mean stays the same. The standard deviation is still 5.
trick: Adding the same number to every value slides the data along without changing its spread, so it stays 5. Only multiplying or dividing would change it.

subject: DA
q: If 60% own cars, 40% bikes, and 25% both, what percent own neither?
solution: Own a car or a bike = 60 + 40 − 25 = 75%, because the 25% who own both were counted twice. Neither = 100% − 75% = 25%, which is 0.25 as a fraction.
trick: 60 + 40 = 100, so the group who own neither is the same size as the group who own both: 25%.

subject: DA
q: Test score frequencies: 10 scored 50, 15 scored 60, 5 scored 70. Find the cumulative frequency ≤60.
solution: Cumulative frequency up to 60 counts everyone who scored 60 or less. That is the 10 who scored 50 plus the 15 who scored 60, so 10 + 15 = 25 students.
trick: Add the frequencies up to 60 and ignore the 70s: 10 + 15 = 25.

subject: DA
q: From a bar chart with maximum height = 25 and minimum height = 5, find the range.
solution: Range = maximum − minimum = 25 − 5 = 20.
trick: Highest bar minus lowest bar: 25 − 5 = 20.

subject: DA
q: If n = 50 and p = 0.7, what is the variance?
solution: Binomial variance = npq = np(1 − p). Here that is 50 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 50 × 0.21 = 10.5.
trick: A binomial variance can never exceed n ÷ 4 = 12.5, because pq is at most 0.25. That rules out 35 and 65 and leaves 10.5.

subject: DA
q: If a dataset follows a normal distribution with mean 50, what is its symmetry point?
solution: A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, and its mean, median and mode all sit at the same centre. So the symmetry point is the mean, 50.
trick: The bell curve mirrors itself about its mean, so the answer is the mean you were given: 50.

subject: DA
q: A binomial experiment has n = 256, p = 0.5. What is the standard deviation?
solution: Standard deviation = √(npq) = √(256 × 0.5 × 0.5) = √64 = 8.
trick: When p = 0.5, the standard deviation is √n ÷ 2. √256 = 16, and half of 16 is 8. The option 16 forgets to halve.

subject: DA
q: A dataset's range is 24, and its maximum is 42. What is the midrange?
solution: Lowest = highest − range = 42 − 24 = 18. Midrange = (highest + lowest) ÷ 2 = (42 + 18) ÷ 2 = 30.
trick: Midrange is the maximum minus half the range: 42 − 12 = 30.

subject: DA
q: A dataset has values: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. What is the mean absolute deviation?
solution: The mean is (10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50) ÷ 5 = 30. The distances from the mean are 20, 10, 0, 10 and 20, which add up to 60. So the mean absolute deviation is 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
trick: The mean is the middle value, 30. The gaps are 20, 10, 0, 10, 20, which total 60, and 60 ÷ 5 = 12.

subject: DA
q: The ages of five siblings are 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. What is their average age?
solution: Mean = sum ÷ number of values = (10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50) ÷ 5 = 150 ÷ 5 = 30.
trick: The ages are evenly spaced, so the mean is the middle one: 30.

subject: DA
q: In a group of 50 students, 30 speak Yoruba, 25 speak Igbo, and 15 speak both. How many speak neither language?
solution: Students who speak at least one language = 30 + 25 − 15 = 40, because the 15 who speak both were counted twice. So neither = 50 − 40 = 10.
trick: 30 + 25 − 15 = 40 speak something, and 50 − 40 = 10 speak neither.

subject: DA

solution: Midpoint = (lower edge + upper edge) ÷ 2 = (15 + 20) ÷ 2 = 35 ÷ 2 = 17.5 kg.
trick: The bin is 5 wide, so go halfway: 15 + 2.5 = 17.5.

subject: DA
q: In a class of 30 students, 18 like math, 12 like physics, and 5 like both. Find how many like neither.
solution: Students who like at least one subject = 18 + 12 − 5 = 25, because the 5 who like both were counted twice. So neither = 30 − 25 = 5 students.
trick: 18 + 12 = 30 is the whole class, so neither is the same size as both: 5.

subject: DA
q: A test has a 5% false positive rate. If 200 healthy people are tested, how many will test positive falsely?
solution: Expected false positives = false positive rate × number of healthy people = 5% × 200 = 0.05 × 200 = 10.
trick: 1% of 200 is 2, so 5% is 10.

subject: DA
q: If the first quartile and third quartile are 10 and 16 respectively, what is the upper outlier threshold?
solution: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 16 − 10 = 6. The upper outlier threshold is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 16 + 1.5 × 6 = 16 + 9 = 25.
trick: The IQR is 6, and 1.5 × 6 = 9. Add that to Q3: 16 + 9 = 25.

subject: DA
q: The weights (in kilograms) of 7 students are: 45,50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 75. What is the range?
solution: Range = largest − smallest = 75 − 45 = 30 kg.
trick: The list is in order, so take the last minus the first: 75 − 45 = 30.

subject: DA
q: The coefficient of variation is 40% for a mean = 650. What is the standard deviation?
solution: Coefficient of variation = standard deviation ÷ mean × 100%. So standard deviation = 40% × 650 = 0.4 × 650 = 260.

subject: DA
q: Frequency: 8 students scored 60, and 12 scored 70. What is the cumulative frequency for scores less than or equal to 70?
solution: Cumulative frequency up to 70 adds the frequencies of all scores up to and including 70. So it is 8 + 12 = 20.
trick: 60 and 70 are the only scores, so it is just everyone: 8 + 12 = 20.

subject: DA
q: Calculate the median of these values: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.
solution: The values are already in order and there are 7 of them, so the median is the (7 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4th value. The 4th value is 8.
trick: Cross off one number from each end until one is left: 3 and 12, 5 and 10, 6 and 9. That leaves 8.

subject: DA
q: What is the total cost if each book costs ₦250 and 12 are bought?

subject: DA
q: IQ is distributed with a mean of 100 and a variance of 225. What is the standard score for an IQ of 130?
solution: Variance = 225, so the standard deviation σ = √225 = 15. Then z = (x − μ) ÷ σ = (130 − 100) ÷ 15 = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.
trick: Take √225 = 15 first, because 225 is the variance. 130 is 30 above the mean, which is two lots of 15.

subject: DA
q: Find what percentage uses only LinkedIn if 80% use LinkedIn, 50% use ResearchGate, and 30% use both.
solution: The 50% for ResearchGate is not needed. Only LinkedIn = all LinkedIn users − those who use both = 80% − 30% = 50%.
trick: Take the overlap out of the LinkedIn circle: 80 − 30 = 50.

subject: DA
q: If 40% of boys choose Maths and 60% of girls do, and half the class are girls, what's P(a random student chose Maths)?
solution: Half the class are girls, so half are boys. P(Maths) = 0.5 × 0.4 + 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5.
trick: The two groups are equal in size, so just average the rates: (40% + 60%) ÷ 2 = 50%.

subject: DA
q: In a positively skewed distribution, which is largest?
showNote: In a positive (right) skew the long right tail pulls the mean up, so mean > median > mode. The show gave Mode.
solution: A positive skew has its long tail on the right, which pulls the mean up the most, so from smallest to largest the usual order is mode, median, mean. The largest is the mean.
trick: The tail drags the mean furthest, so with positive skew the mean is the biggest (with negative skew it is the smallest).

subject: DA
q: A bag has 3 red and 7 black balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. If the second ball is red, find the probability that the first ball is also red.
solution: P(first red | second red) = P(both red) ÷ P(second red). P(both red) = 3/10 × 2/9 = 6/90 and P(second red) = 6/90 + 7/10 × 3/9 = 27/90, so the answer is 6/27 = 2/9.
trick: Fix the second ball as red. The first ball then comes from the other 9, and 2 of those 9 are red, so 2/9.

subject: DA
q: For the data: 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, determine the interquartile range.
solution: There are 7 values, so the median is the 4th (20). Leaving the median out, the lower half 8, 12, 16 has median Q1 = 12 and the upper half 24, 28, 32 has median Q3 = 28. So IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 28 − 12 = 16.
trick: With 7 values, Q1 is the 2nd value (12) and Q3 is the 6th (28), which are 4 steps of 4 apart, so 16.

solution: The 75th percentile is the value that 75% of the data fall below. So 75% scored below 45.

subject: DA
q: A confusion matrix is used in
solution: A confusion matrix counts correct and wrong predictions for each class (true and false positives and negatives), while regression predicts numbers, not classes. So it is used in classification.

subject: DA
q: Players A and B serve properly with probs 0.8 and 0.9. If server is equally likely, what's P(serve proper)?

trick: The chances are equal, so average 0.8 and 0.9 to get 0.85.

solution: Order the nine values: 4, 5, 9, 11, 13, 15, 15, 17, 18. The 5th value is the median, 13, and the value that appears most often is 15 (twice). So the median is 13 and the mode is 15.
trick: Spot the repeat first: only 15 appears twice, so the mode is 15, and only the option '13, 15' ends in 15.

trick: No sums needed: the set with the widest spread, 2 to 11, has the largest SD.

The question gives 2 for the original, although the population SD of 10, 12, 14, 16 works out to √5 ≈ 2.24. Either way the new SD equals the old one, so it is 2.
trick: Adding a constant never changes the SD, so it is the same as the original: 2.
